newsitem.title: USA: CBOT delivery changes attract range of comments.
newsitem.headline: CBOT delivery changes attract range of comments.

text.p: Here are some excerpts from the more than 250 letters sent to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission about the Chicago Board of Trade's proposed changes to delivery terms in its corn and soybean contracts:
CARGILL INC
Norman Hay, president of Cargill's North American grain operations, said in a March 24 letter to the CFTC that the proposed changes would "worsen the already tenuous situation."

-- the river-only delivery terms will create "a greater potential for price manipulation," Cargill said, adding that the proposed terms do not reflect cash market realities. "The deliverable capacity that is being touted in this working alternative is misleading," Cargill said. "The terms of the contract, notably price differentials and loading terms, will discourage deliveries."

-- Cargill said it supported an alternative delivery mechanism suggested by the CFTC in a letter to the CBOT last year. The agency's suggestion, which added a shipping certificate river delivery system and had price differentials at delivery points that reflected the cash market "would be a sound approach to the dilemma we face today," the company said. "We should leave Toledo in the system but price it economically."
THE ANDERSONS INC
Michael Anderson, president of The Andersons, told the CFTC in a March 18 letter that the CBOT proposal was not in the best interest of hedgers on the exchange.

-- "Ownership of delivery facilities in the proposed delivery area is highly concentrated," the Andersons said. "The financial requirements included in the proposal will add to that concentration by eliminating smaller companies." The company also said market transparency would "be lost with a shipping certificate proposal exclusively along the Northern Illinois River."

-- The company said it preferred delivery changes that would maintain Toledo as a delivery point; add a 4/2 barge loading plan for Chicago; maintain a warehouse receipt system for Toledo and Chicago with a $03.6 per month storage rate; eliminate the December corn contract and replace it with November and January; and establish price differentials for Illinois River delivery locations at a rate reflecting 150 percent of the barge tariff.
LOUIS DREYFUS CORP
Bruce Ritter, executive vice president of Dreyfus, said the company is a long hedger in the nearby futures months to protect its short sales positions and often takes delivery of contracts.

-- "Tying ourselves to a barge-dominated contract is asking for trouble," the company said in an April 1 letter. "Despite the twofold increase in delivery capacity under the CBOT's proposal, the quality of this capacity will increase not decrease our present concerns over the uncertainty of deliverable supplies."

-- Dreyfus said it preferred a plan that would maintain Toledo and Chicago as receipt-based delivery points and add the Northern Illinois River shipping certificates but limit deliveries to 7 days of capacity.
CONTINENTAL GRAIN CO

Thomas Coyle, vice president of Continental Grain Co, said his company supported the CBOT proposal as improving effectiveness for hedgers. Continental said it has six barge loading facilities on the northern Illinois River.

-- The CBOT proposed changes "improves the dependability of deliveries throughout the market year," the company said in an April 1 letter to the CFTC. The Illinois River locations would add some 90 million bushels for a total deliverable capacity of 146 million bushels, versus 56 million bushels capacity in Toledo.

-- "The net worth requirements are not a significant factor for four of the six companies that represent 90 percent of the delivery capacity in the shipping area," Continental said. The other two companies could enter into a joint venture or lease arrangement to qualify.

-- A single delivery system means more transparency because barge freight and cash markets are "generally well defined in the open market." The single delivery system would also provide hedgers in the west and the east neither an unfair advantage or disadvantage. ----------
BUNGE CORP
Richard Kerwin, senior vice president of Bunge Corp in St. Louis, said the proposed changes would be a "major improvement" by making the market more transparent.

-- The changes would reduce the likelihood that futures prices would be affected by logistical impediment, the company said. "Pure economics would be best served by avoiding committees which study and recommend changes in delivery differentials," Kerwin said in an April 11 letter to the CFTC. "We would have preferred that the single delivery location be subdivided but provided with a mechanism to automatically adjust the differentials between subdivisions over time if actual delivery volumes indicated that any subdivision were economically favored by the differentials in place."
((-- Washington commodities desk, 202-898-8467))
